title: You Should Stay in Education for a Long Time, But There Is One Catch
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart offers two truths for teachers in a season of turmoil. First, commit to education long-term, because expert teaching is hard-earned and the career educator's work echoes across generations. Second, a long career guarantees hard change, since US education has high turnover and bosses, courses, curricula and standards come and go. His move is to ground resilience in what is constant: the work is rich because it is teaching, not because of a particular boss or course. He frames this as realistic idealism, neither cynical nor naive, and keeps the focus on the long-term flourishing of kids.
points: Expertise in teaching takes years of practice, study, collaboration and humility, so leaving after a few years forfeits the rewards of mastery.
Teachers should prioritize developing expertise in the highest-impact areas first when preparing for the long haul.
High teacher and administrator turnover makes education unusually changeable, so favorite bosses and treasured courses should be enjoyed but not leaned on.
Resilience comes from locating the richness of the work in teaching itself rather than in any boss, course or program.
Realistic idealism is the stance: avoid cynicism while expecting that stable conditions will not last.
quotes: First, I think we all ought to make it our goal to commit to education long-term. It's incredibly difficult to become an expert teacher. Expertise in this field, like all professional fields, is hard-earned, requiring years of earnest work, practice, study, collaboration, and humility.

The career educator is a person whose life's work creates an eternal echo; the generations that you'll change through spending decades in schools working toward the long-term good of kids… they'll go on to change generations long after you're gone. What a thing to spend your life's work on.
Second, sticking around is certain to bring hard changes and tough seasons. All professions are rocked by change — more now, I'm sure, than in less technological times.

That course you cherish? Enjoy it while it's there, and leverage it with all your might toward the long-term good of your students. But courses and curricula and standards and programs change all the time. Be ready.

I'm cautious in writing all this because the goal ISN'T to grow cynical or pessimistic. Realistic idealism is what we're after. This builds in us the resilience to keep going, sustainably, even when times are tumultuous, or everyone around us is insane with neomania

The work is the long-term flourishing of kids. It's nice when the work is convenient, when administrative or curricular stability gives us ideal conditions within which to work. But this season, too, is bound to turn at some point.
